Pixel

Pixel provides owned image buffers, image codecs and transforms, vector-style drawing primitives, text layout, colors, brushes, paths, and OpenGL or software renderers.

Most image operations mutate an Pixel.Image in place. Pixel coordinates use an origin at the top-left; x grows to the right and y grows downward. Dimensions and integer coordinates are expressed in pixels unless a declaration says otherwise. Colors use straight (non-premultiplied) alpha.

Create and save an image

using Pixel var image = Image.create(320, 180, .RGBA8) image.fill(Color.fromRgb(24, 32, 48)) try image.save("preview.png")

Record and render with the CPU backend

Create the concrete backend first, borrow it as an Pixel.IRenderer, then create the Pixel.Painter with that renderer. The painter records commands; Pixel.Painter.render submits them to the renderer selected at creation.

var cpu: RenderCpu let renderer: IRenderer = &cpu var painter = Painter.create(renderer) var context = try renderer.createContext(null, 320, 180) defer renderer.deleteContext(&context) renderer.begin(context) painter.begin() painter.clear(Color.fromRgb(24, 32, 48)) painter.fillCircle(160, 90, 48, Color.fromRgb(72, 149, 239)) painter.end() painter.render() renderer.end() let image = cpu.surfaceImage()

The filename extension selects the encoder when loading or saving. Operations that can reject malformed data, fail to access a file, or fail in a backend use Swag's normal fail mechanism.

Getting started

Pixel covers two related jobs: manipulating owned images on the CPU and recording two-dimensional drawing commands for a renderer. Start with the smallest layer that solves the problem.

GoalStart with
Load, transform, or encode pixelsPixel.Image
Express a colorPixel.Color and Pixel.Argb
Draw shapes, paths, textures, or textPixel.Painter
Build reusable vector geometryPixel.LinePath and Pixel.LinePathList
Write backend-independent rendering codePixel.IRenderer
Render recorded commands with OpenGLPixel.RenderOgl
Render deterministic pixels without a GPUPixel.RenderCpu
Draw into an image without managing a framePixel.ImageCanvas
Load and lay out fontsPixel.TypeFace, Pixel.Font, and Pixel.RichString

A first image

An Pixel.Image owns a tightly packed, row-major pixel buffer. The pixel format determines how many bytes belong to each pixel.

using Pixel var image = Image.create(320, 180, .RGBA8) image.fill(Color.fromRgb(24, 32, 48)) try image.save("preview.png")

Image operations that change dimensions or encoding update the same value. Copying an image copies its owned bytes; it does not create a shared view.

For vector drawing, create a concrete renderer, borrow it as an Pixel.IRenderer, and pass that interface to Pixel.Painter.create. The renderer owns textures and targets; the painter only records the commands that refer to them. See Rendering recorded commands for complete CPU and OpenGL lifecycles.

Coordinate and color conventions

Pixel coordinates start at the top-left. x grows to the right and y grows downward. Unless a declaration says otherwise, dimensions, positions, stroke widths, and font sizes are expressed in pixels.

Pixel.Color stores straight alpha. A transparent color therefore retains its RGB components; blending and render targets decide how those components contribute to the destination.

Note

Operations that can reject input, access files, allocate backend resources, or compile shaders use Swag's normal fail mechanism. Propagate those failures with try, or handle them at the boundary of your application.

Images and codecs

Pixel.Image is the center of the CPU image API. It owns its storage and carries the geometry and Pixel.PixelFormat needed to interpret every row.

Load, transform, save

The filename extension selects the decoder or encoder. Built-in decoding covers BMP, DDS, EXR, GIF, ICO, JPEG, KTX2, PNG, PSD, QOI, TGA, TIFF, and WebP. Every format but PSD also has a built-in encoder where the container has a useful flattened-image writing contract.

using Pixel var image = try Image.load("portrait.png") image.crop(40, 20, 640, 640) image.resize(256, 256, .Bilinear) try image.save("avatar.png")

crop, resize, flip, filters, and channel operations mutate the image. This makes a processing pipeline read naturally and avoids a chain of short-lived image values.

Choose a pixel format

Use Pixel.PixelFormat RGBA8 for general-purpose color with alpha and RGB8 when opacity is guaranteed. RGB16/RGBA16 retain normalized 16-bit samples; the F16 and F32 families retain HDR values. Each precision also has compact Gray and GrayAlpha storage for masks, distance fields, and luminance images. Query Pixel.PixelFormat.bitsPerPixel, Pixel.PixelFormat.channels, and Pixel.PixelFormat.hasAlpha when generic code must adapt to the encoding.

All packed formats can be converted with Pixel.Image.convertTo or copied with Pixel.Image.convertedTo. Converting to an integer format clamps and quantizes; converting to grayscale uses luminance; adding alpha creates opaque samples; removing alpha discards it. Floating-point conversions preserve finite HDR values until an integer destination requires clamping.

Packed image and texture storage supports these precisions. Painter render targets remain straight-alpha RGBA8; convert their readback explicitly when a high-precision processing pipeline is required.

Pixel.AlphaMode records whether stored colors are straight or premultiplied. Use Pixel.Image.convertAlphaTo when crossing an API boundary with a different alpha convention. Filters and resampling preserve this association, and encoders write straight-alpha file samples.

FieldMeaning
width, heightImage extent in pixels
rowStrideByte stride of one tightly packed row
pixelsOwned row-major bytes
pixelFormatEncoding of each pixel
alphaModeStraight or premultiplied alpha association
metadataCodec metadata preserved when supported
Warning

Low-level access through pixels must honor pixelFormat, bytesPerPixel, and rowStride. Prefer the typed image operations unless direct byte access is required.

Codec precision

PNG preserves 8- and 16-bit grayscale or RGB samples with optional alpha. EXR preserves half- and full-float Y, YA, RGB, and RGBA scanlines. DDS and KTX2 preserve their supported uncompressed integer and floating layouts; their decoders also read BC1 through BC5 block-compressed textures. Other general-purpose codecs convert to the nearest supported 8-bit RGB/RGBA representation.

The PSD decoder imports the flattened composite from PSD version 1 RGB or grayscale files with 8- or 16-bit raw or PackBits channel data. An optional alpha channel is retained. Layers, masks, CMYK/Lab color modes, effects, and PSB files are rejected instead of being silently flattened or misinterpreted.

Encoding options

Pass the encoder-specific options value as the second argument of Pixel.Image.save. A null option value selects the encoder defaults. Decode limits and requested output behavior belong in Pixel.DecodeOptions when loading untrusted or unusually large files.

Vector drawing

Pixel.Painter records a deferred command stream. A drawing scope always follows the same shape: begin, issue commands, end, then submit the painter to a renderer.

using Pixel var cpu: RenderCpu let renderer: IRenderer = &cpu var painter = Painter.create(renderer) painter.begin() painter.clear(Color.fromRgb(18, 20, 28)) painter.fillRoundRect(24, 24, 220, 96, 14, 14, Color.fromRgb(62, 132, 220)) painter.drawRect(24, 24, 220, 96, Color.fromRgb(230, 240, 255), 2) painter.end()

begin clears previously recorded vertices and commands and restores the default drawing state. Pixel.Painter.render submits the finished stream to the renderer selected by Pixel.Painter.create. A default-initialized painter remains useful for command inspection and goldens, but it cannot render or allocate a Pixel.Layer until Pixel.Painter.setRenderer is called.

Paths

Use Pixel.LinePath for one contour and Pixel.LinePathList for several contours. A path starts at one point, accepts line, curve, Bézier, or arc segments, and may be closed before filling.

var path: LinePath path.start(80, 16) path.lineTo(144, 128) path.lineTo(16, 128) path.close() painter.begin() painter.fillPath(&path, Color.fromRgb(245, 190, 48)) painter.drawPath(&path, Color.fromRgb(80, 54, 10), 2) painter.end()

Brushes and pens

Pixel.Brush describes fills: solid colors, textures, hatches, and linear, radial, or sweep gradients. Pixel.Pen adds stroke width, joins, end caps, and dash behavior around a brush.

Blend modes

Pixel.Painter.setBlendingMode controls how later drawing combines with the current target. Besides direct framebuffer operations, Pixel.BlendingMode provides the standard separable modes such as Multiply, Screen, Overlay, and SoftLight, plus the non-separable Hue, Saturation, Color, and Luminosity modes. They blend straight source and backdrop colors, then apply source-over coverage.

The artistic equations use destination alpha as backdrop coverage. Because a new painter writes RGB but preserves alpha by default, initialize an opaque surface with a full channel mask before selecting these modes. clear obeys the current color mask.

painter.setColorMaskFull() painter.clear(Color.fromRgb(24, 30, 42)) painter.setColorMaskColor() painter.pushState() painter.setBlendingMode(.Multiply) painter.fillCircle(96, 72, 48, Color.fromArgb(180, Argb.RoyalBlue)) painter.setBlendingMode(.Screen) painter.fillCircle(132, 72, 48, Color.fromArgb(180, Argb.Tomato)) painter.popState()

Pixel.RenderCpu supports every mode. Before using an artistic mode with an unknown OpenGL context, query Pixel.RenderOgl.supportsAdvancedBlending after renderer initialization. Min and Max remain raw component equations; use Darken and Lighten for source-over artistic blending with partial alpha.

Use Pixel.Painter.pushState and Pixel.Painter.popState around local changes to transforms, clipping, blending, interpolation, or quality. This keeps a component's drawing code independent from its caller.

Tip

Build reusable geometry once, then vary the brush, pen, transform, and clipping state when recording each frame.

Text and mathematical layout

Text has three layers. Pixel.TypeFace owns font-file data, Pixel.Font selects a size and rendering mode, and Pixel.Painter records shaped glyphs. Use Pixel.RichString when a paragraph needs style runs, wrapping, alignment, or hit-testable links.

Load a font

using Pixel let font = try Font.create("Inter-Regular.ttf", 20) var painter: Painter painter.begin() painter.drawString(24, 32, "Hello, Pixel", font, Color.fromRgb(245, 245, 245)) painter.end()

Pixel.FontRenderMode Auto chooses between bitmap and multi-channel signed-distance-field rendering according to the effective on-screen size. Select a specific mode only when stable atlas behavior or a particular rendering technique matters more than automatic quality.

Rich text

Pixel.RichString.set parses Pixel's lightweight inline markup. Pixel.RichString.compute rebuilds shaped chunks after text or layout inputs change, and Pixel.Painter.drawRichString records the result.

Keep the Pixel.FontFamily and formatting inputs alive while computing and drawing the text. The rich string retains its source text and derived layout state, so it can be reused until one of those inputs changes.

Mathematical expressions

Parse notation with Pixel.MathExpression.parse, measure it with Pixel.MathExpression.measure, and draw it through Pixel.Painter.drawMath. For one-off trusted strings, Pixel.Painter.drawMathLatex combines parsing, layout, and drawing.

Note

Mathematical layout supports a practical TeX-like subset, not a complete TeX engine. Parse failures identify unsupported or malformed input through the normal fail path.

Rendering recorded commands

Pixel separates four roles:

RoleAPI
Own backend state and resourcesPixel.RenderCpu, Pixel.RenderOgl, or another implementation
Expose backend-independent operationsPixel.IRenderer
Describe one drawable and its dimensionsPixel.RenderContext
Record one deferred command streamPixel.Painter

There is no central renderer registry or closed backend enum. Any type that implements Pixel.IRenderer is available immediately. Keep the concrete value alive, borrow it as the interface, and create each painter with that interface:

var cpu: RenderCpu let renderer: IRenderer = &cpu var painter = Painter.create(renderer)

The interface, painter, contexts, textures, and render targets do not own the concrete renderer. They must not outlive it. Resources also stay tied to the renderer that created them and cannot be moved to another backend.

CPU frame lifecycle

Pixel.RenderCpu needs no native window, display server, GPU, or driver. Its output is deterministic and Pixel.RenderCpu.surfaceImage returns an owned copy of the current surface.

var cpu: RenderCpu let renderer: IRenderer = &cpu var painter = Painter.create(renderer) var context = try renderer.createContext(null, 320, 180) defer renderer.deleteContext(&context) renderer.init() renderer.begin(context) painter.begin() painter.clear(Color.fromRgb(20, 22, 30)) painter.fillRect({24, 24, 120, 48}, Color.fromRgb(60, 140, 240)) painter.end() painter.render() renderer.end() let image = cpu.surfaceImage()

The concrete Pixel.RenderCpu.begin overload taking width and height is a convenience for CPU-only code. The interface/context form above is preferable when the caller can work with any renderer.

OpenGL frame lifecycle

Pixel.RenderOgl uses the same interface. Pass the platform window handle to Pixel.IRenderer.createContext, make the first context current, then initialize renderer-owned OpenGL resources. A context created with shared uses the same renderer resources as that earlier context.

var ogl: RenderOgl let renderer: IRenderer = &ogl var painter = Painter.create(renderer) var context = try renderer.createContext( cast(#null const *void) window.nativeHandle, width, height) defer renderer.deleteContext(&context) renderer.setCurrentContext(context) renderer.init() renderer.begin(context) painter.begin() // Record shapes, textures, and text here. painter.end() painter.render() renderer.end()

Update Pixel.RenderContext.width and Pixel.RenderContext.height after a drawable resize. Keep OpenGL calls on the thread required by the platform integration.

Render targets and layers

Use Pixel.RenderTarget for a manually managed off-screen pass. Pixel.Layer packages temporary targets, supersampling, resolution, blur, and composition. A layer obtains its renderer from the painter, so its call site does not repeat or risk contradicting backend selection:

var layer: Layer layer.begin(&painter, {width: 320, height: 180}) // Record layer content with painter. layer.end() layer.draw({dstRect: {0, 0, 320, 180}})

Textures created by Pixel.IRenderer.addImage and targets created by Pixel.IRenderer.createRenderTarget belong to that renderer. Release them through the same interface. CPU and OpenGL handles are not interchangeable.

Pixel goldens

Pixel.Testing.assertImageGolden stores a rendered PNG beside the calling test. The default comparison is exact; pass Pixel.Testing.ImageGoldenOptions only when a workflow has a justified bounded tolerance.

let image = cpu.surfaceImage() Testing.assertImageGolden(&image, "toolbar.enabled")

The first run creates goldens/toolbar.enabled.png and passes so the new file can be reviewed. A mismatch fails and writes toolbar.enabled.actual.png. After reviewing both images, swc tools\goldens.swgs promotes pending snapshots.

Use Pixel.Testing.assertImagesNear when two backends render the same scene in one test. It writes both images on failure. The channel-delta limit absorbs small rounding differences; the different-pixel limit separately bounds raster-edge outliers, so neither tolerance can hide a broad rendering regression.

Pixel.RenderCpu interprets built-in shapes, brushes, textures, clipping, blending, bitmap and MSDF text effects, render targets, blur, and supersampling. Custom GLSL shaders remain OpenGL-only. Keep a small OpenGL integration suite for shader compiler, driver, context, and presentation coverage, and compare its portable scenes with CPU output.

Warning

End a painter before calling Pixel.Painter.render. Do not mutate its command or vertex buffers while a renderer is consuming them.

struct Bmp.Header #src

Represents the Windows BITMAPINFOHEADER binary layout.

Fields retain the names and units defined by the BMP file format. The structure can also be used when exchanging DIB data with Windows APIs.

#[Swag.Pack(1)] struct Header

Bits stored for one pixel.

Number of important palette entries, or zero when all are important.

Number of palette entries used, or zero for the format default.

biCompressionu32

Compression mode, such as BI_RGB or BI_BITFIELDS.

biHeights32

Signed height; a negative value denotes top-down rows.

biPlanesu16

Number of color planes; valid BMP data uses 1.

biSizeu32

Size of this header in bytes.

struct Clipper.Transform #src

Performs integer polygon clipping and Boolean operations.

Add subject and clip paths with addPath, then call execute. The structure is opaque because its edge graph and scanline state are implementation details.

Example

var subject: Clipper.ClipperPath subject.add({x: 0, y: 0}) subject.add({x: 100, y: 0}) subject.add({x: 100, y: 80}) subject.add({x: 0, y: 80}) var transform: Clipper.Transform transform.addPath(&subject, .Subject) var solution: Clipper.ClipperPaths transform.execute(.Union, &solution, .NonZero, .NonZero)
#[Swag.Opaque] struct Transform

Methods

NameDescription
opDrop

Releases edge and record storage owned by the transform.

Field details

blurRadius#

Blur radius (in pixels) applied to the saliency map for smoothing. Range: 0–5 (typical 2–4). Higher = smoother gradients, less fine detail.

centerWeight#

Weight for proximity to the image center (center bias). Range: 0.0–0.3 (typical 0.05–0.15). 0.0 removes center preference.

edgePenalty#

Penalty for crops that cut through strong edges (uses edge-distance map). Range: 0.0–0.5 (typical 0.10–0.25). 0.0 disables the edge term.

faceWeight#

Reserved for future face detection bonus when faces are inside the crop. Range: 0.0–1.0 (currently unused).

maxSearchSteps#

Number of scale steps in multi-scale search. Range: 5–20 (typical 8–12). More = more thorough but slower.

maxSize#

Maximum working image size (pixels) for the longest side when computing crops/scores. 0 (or <=0) disables downscaling. The original image is always used for the final crop.

minCoverage#

Minimum fraction of the original image area the crop must keep. Range: 0.0–1.0. Lower allows tighter crops; higher preserves more context. Special: >= 0.95 triggers fast single-scale mode (no multi-scale search).

shrinkPrior#

Prior favoring larger crops (adds an area-proportional bonus). Range: 0.0–0.3 (typical 0.05–0.15). 0.0 means no size preference.

strideFrac#

Search stride as a fraction of the crop size (per axis). Range: 0.01–0.20 (typical 0.06–0.12). Lower = slower, higher quality.

thirdsWeight#

Weight for the rule-of-thirds compositional bonus. Range: 0.0–0.5 (typical 0.15–0.25). 0.0 disables thirds influence.

struct Pixel.FillPreparer #src

Builds the tessellation a fill would build, without recording anything.

A fill caches its triangulation inside the contours it fills, so the frame that first draws a shape pays for it and the frames after it do not. That is what makes drawing an unchanged document cheap — and what makes the first frame at a new scale expensive, because flattening the geometry finer replaces the contours every cached tessellation was keyed on. A consumer that knows ahead of the frame what it is about to draw, and at what scale — a document viewer that has just decoded a page, or one whose window has just been resized — can pay that here instead, and on whatever thread it likes: nothing below reads a painter, a renderer, or any state shared between them.

The preparer owns the workspaces the build needs, so preparing a page's worth of shapes allocates once rather than once per shape. One preparer serves one thread, and the geometry it is given must not be drawn while it is preparing it.

var preparer: FillPreparer for shape in page do preparer.prepare(shape, scale, .NonZero)
#[Swag.Opaque] struct FillPreparer

Methods

NameDescription

Flattens a path for a draw at scale, without tessellating anything.

prepare

Prepares what Pixel.Painter.fillPath under rule would build for pathList.

struct Pixel.FontCache #src

Owns the glyph storage and the font views created through it.

Each renderer owns one cache and every font it hands out lives and dies with it. An OpenGL renderer also uploads atlas pixels to context-owned textures; Pixel.RenderCpu samples the atlas bytes directly. Code that only measures or lays out text can own a bare cache with no renderer at all.

A cache holds a handful of entries (one per typeface, size and style actually drawn), so lookups walk them rather than hashing a key. That keeps font creation allocation-free on the draw path, which matters because an automatic font resolves a concrete view on every run it draws.

#[Swag.NoCopy] struct FontCache

Drops every glyph cache and font view created through this cache.

struct Pixel.ImageCanvas #src

Draws into an image with the full painter, without a window.

A canvas owns a CPU renderer and the render target behind it, so a program that only writes files can render paths, brushes, gradients, textures, text, clipping, blending, and transforms and read the result back as pixels. The same backend powers display-independent image generation and pixel tests.

Record into Pixel.ImageCanvas.painter, then call Pixel.ImageCanvas.toImage. A canvas can be reused: drawing again after a read starts a new frame over a cleared target.

Example

var canvas = try ImageCanvas.create(256, 256) canvas.clear(Color.fromRgb(11, 11, 13)) var path: LinePath path.start(32, 32) path.lineTo(224, 32) path.lineTo(128, 224) path.close() canvas.painter.fillPath(&path, Color.fromRgb(247, 249, 0)) var image = try canvas.toImage() try image.save("triangle.png")

struct Pixel.ImageFormat #src

Names one image file format and the filename extensions that select it.

An encoder or a decoder declares this once, and the registry derives extension matching from it: Pixel.Image.canSave, Pixel.Image.canLoad and the codec lookup all read the same declaration, so a codec cannot claim an extension its format does not list.

A user interface enumerates the supported formats with Pixel.Image.encodableFormats or Pixel.Image.decodableFormats and builds its file filters from them.

NameTypeDescription

Accepted extensions, lowercase, dot-prefixed, separated by ;.

namestring

Display name of the format, such as PNG - Portable Network Graphics.

Field details

extensions#

Accepted extensions, lowercase, dot-prefixed, separated by ;.

The first one is canonical: it is the extension a file dialog appends when the user types a bare name. .jpg;.jpeg is a format with two spellings, not two formats. The separator matches the filter convention of the gui file dialog, so the field can be handed to it unchanged.

name#

Display name of the format, such as PNG - Portable Network Graphics.

It is a literal with static storage, so a user interface can hold it without copying it. It is deliberately not translated: these are format names.

Reports whether this format claims fileName, by its extension alone.

Stores one opaque metadata record associated with an image.

Codecs use signature and tag to identify a record and keep value as its format-specific byte payload. Unknown records can therefore survive a decode/encode round trip without Pixel interpreting their contents.

Structured TagBin payloads are decoded through the statically requested type, so the source type name is not part of this record's persisted identity.

struct Pixel.MathExpression #src

Stores a parsed, reusable mathematical expression.

The accepted input is a practical LaTeX math subset; no surrounding $ delimiters are needed. It includes:

  • grouped rows, Unicode literals, sub/superscripts and TeX atom spacing;
  • fractions, binomials, indexed roots, scalable delimiters and common accents;
  • Greek letters, relations, arrows, named functions and large operators/limits;
  • roman/italic/bold/text runs and explicit TeX spacing;
  • matrix, pmatrix, bmatrix, Bmatrix, vmatrix, Vmatrix, cases and aligned.

Parse expressions once when they are drawn repeatedly:

Example

var expression = try Pixel.MathExpression.parse(#raw "\frac{x_i^2}{\sqrt{1+x}}") let metrics = painter.drawMath(20, 30, &expression, font, Pixel.Argb.MidnightBlue)
#[Swag.Opaque] struct MathExpression

struct Pixel.Painter #src

Records drawing operations as a deferred command and vertex stream.

Create it with an Pixel.IRenderer, call Painter.begin, issue drawing operations, call Painter.end, then call Painter.render. Coordinates are in path-space pixels and are transformed by the current Core.Math.Transform2.

var cpu: RenderCpu let renderer: IRenderer = &cpu var painter = Painter.create(renderer) painter.begin() painter.clear(Color.fromRgb(24, 32, 48)) painter.fillCircle(48, 48, 24, Color.fromRgb(72, 149, 239)) painter.end()

struct Pixel.Pen #src

Describes how a path is stroked.

Lengths and scale factors are expressed in path-space pixels. Use the factory functions for common solid, dashed, and hatched pens.

A non-zero outlineSize adds a border of that width outside the stroke. The border is the stroke's own silhouette pushed out, so it keeps the same width along the shaft, around every join and cap, and along each dash, instead of being a second, proportionally larger stroke.

struct Pixel.RenderCpu #src

Executes Pixel.Painter command streams into deterministic CPU-owned pixel buffers.

A CPU renderer owns every texture and render target it creates. It needs no native window, graphics context, or GPU driver. Call Pixel.RenderCpu.begin, record and submit a painter, then read the surface or an off-screen target back as an Pixel.Image.

Every renderer-independent painter operation, including MSDF font effects, blur, and supersampling resolve, is interpreted directly. Custom OpenGL shaders remain specific to Pixel.RenderOgl and are a programmer error when submitted to this backend.

struct Pixel.RenderOgl #src

A renderer is non-copyable and owns its shaders, textures, buffers, and queued render targets. Create it as an Pixel.IRenderer, create a Pixel.RenderContext, call init, then bracket frames with begin and end. The artistic blend modes use advanced blend equations, with explicit barriers when the context does not provide coherent ordering; call Pixel.RenderOgl.supportsAdvancedBlending after init before selecting one on a context whose driver capabilities are not known.

Field details

fonts#

Glyph storage and font views of this renderer. A glyph atlas carries a GPU texture created in this renderer's context, so it must not outlive it: fonts are created through this cache and released with the renderer.

scratchClearedPixels#

Device pixels the overlap-safe path has cleared as alpha scratch, and what the same batches would have cleared had each been given the whole clipping rectangle.

The pair is what makes the bound measurable from a single run: the second is the cost of the unbounded behaviour, on the very geometry the first was measured on. Reset them with Pixel.RenderOgl.resetScratchCounters.

Configures face, outline, glow, shadow, and bevel effects for MSDF text.

The face effects are derived from the glyph distance field and share one draw. The soft drop shadow uses an offset second pass. struct Pixel.Yuv420View #src

One picture in planar 4:2:0, borrowed from whatever produced it.

Every video codec reconstructs this layout: full-resolution luma and two chroma planes at half resolution on both axes, so one chroma sample serves a two-by-two block of pixels. A view owns nothing and stays valid only while the planes behind it do.

The offsets are already applied, so a cropped picture is described by pointing the planes at its visible corner. A 4:2:0 crop is always an even number of luma samples — the format states it in chroma units — which is what lets the chroma plane be addressed at half the coordinates.

Rows run top-down: the plane pointers address the top-left visible sample, which is the order every codec reconstructs a picture in. Pixel.Image stores its rows the other way round, so a conversion into one writes them in reverse, and a renderer that samples the planes directly accounts for the difference itself.

struct Yuv420View

struct Svg.Document #src

Builds a vector document and writes it as SVG text.

The document holds filled paths in the coordinate space it was created with; nothing is rasterized, so the result stays sharp at any size. Straight and Bézier segments are written as their exact SVG commands, while a path holding an arc or a smoothed curve is written from its flattened contour, so the file always describes the same shape the rasterizer draws.

Example

var path: LinePath path.start(8, 8) path.lineTo(56, 8) path.lineTo(32, 56) path.close() var doc = Svg.Document.create(64, 64) doc.setBackground(Color.fromRgb(11, 11, 13)) doc.addPath(path, Color.fromRgb(247, 249, 0)) try doc.save("mark.svg")

struct Svg.Drawing #src

A parsed vector document, ready to paint at any scale.

Pixel.Svg.Drawing.parse reads the SVG subset used by standalone artwork and the standard themes: basic shapes and paths, groups, definitions, uses, symbols and their viewports, clipping paths, start/mid/end markers, linear and centered radial gradients with their inheritance chains, repeating patterns, text runs with letter and word spacing, bounded raster images, a Gaussian blur followed by offsets or a standalone drop shadow, CSS Color 3 solid paints, opacity, path-length-calibrated stroke dashes, the complete affine transform list, and simple element/class/id style rules.

Masks, radial focal points, arbitrary font fallback and the remaining SVG filter primitives are out of contract; a font-family list is reduced to serif, monospace or the default face rather than resolved against installed fonts. Because vector geometry is not rasterized at parse time, the same drawing renders sharply at any size.

struct Svg.ParseOptions #src

Controls resources that SVG parsing may resolve outside the document text.

Data-image URIs are accepted up to maxImageBytes. A non-empty externalResourceRoot additionally permits relative raster-image references whose canonical path remains inside that directory; absolute paths and escaping .. references are rejected.

The three typeface names select what font-family resolves to. A document names faces the machine may not carry, so a family list is reduced to the class it asks for — serif, monospace, or anything else — exactly as the HTML view reduces it, and the class selects one of these files. Each may be a file path or a filename from the system font directory; a name that fails to load falls back to fontFileName.

struct ParseOptions

enum Pixel.PaintParams #src

Controls optional painter behaviors.

#[Swag.EnumFlags] enum PaintParams

Cases

NameDescription
Antialiased

Generate coverage fringes along vector edges.

Default

Use the normal antialiased configuration.

DistanceStrokes

Antialias a stroke from the fragment's distance to its centre line instead of from a

Zero

Disable every optional behavior.

Case details

DistanceStrokes#

Antialias a stroke from the fragment's distance to its centre line instead of from a fringe band extruded along each side.

A banded segment costs a quad and a band on each of its long edges, eighteen vertices; a measured segment costs its two triangles. A document of strokes is bound by that emission, so the saving is close to the ratio. What moves in exchange is the edge itself: the band pair carries a solid core out to the full half width and softens beyond it, while the distance places the same contour there and softens across it, which reads a shade finer. Turn it on for content whose weight is its own, and compare before making it a default.

enum Pixel.PixelFormat #src

Describes the channel set, sample representation, byte order, and storage class of a picture.

Every format but one packs its channels into consecutive bytes of one row. Yuv420 does not: it is what a video codec reconstructs, and it stores luma at full resolution beside two chroma planes at half resolution on both axes, so one chroma sample serves a two-by-two block. Ask Pixel.PixelFormat.isPacked before treating a format as bytes per pixel; Pixel.Image holds packed formats only, and a planar picture is described by Pixel.Yuv420View.

MSDF distance range in atlas texels mapped to the stored [0,1] range.

const Pixel.StrokeCoverageBias #src

Antialiasing fringe half-width, in (untransformed) path-space pixels.

Where a measured stroke's coverage lives in the vertex coverage attribute.

The attribute normally carries an extruded band's ramp, one inside the contour and zero on the outer edge. A measured stroke needs a signed distance instead, because one quad has to describe both of its sides, and the two meanings have to travel in the same batch so a stroke and the joins and caps around it still draw together. They are told apart by range: a band never leaves zero to one, so a measured stroke is written around this bias, and any value above half of it is read as a distance. The contour sits half a unit either side of the bias, which puts the signed distance on the same scale as the ramp it replaces and leaves the screen-space coverage both backends derive from it unchanged.

const StrokeCoverageBias = 4.0'f32

func Color.ensureContrast #src

Adjusts the color to meet a required contrast ratio against target.

The result meets or exceeds requiredContrast using the WCAG contrast calculation. The function iteratively darkens or lightens the color in the direction that increases contrast most effectively.

  • Parameters:
    • target: The color to contrast against (e.g., foreground or background).
    • requiredContrast: The minimum contrast ratio (default = 4.5 for normal text).
    • step: Brightness adjustment per iteration. Positive values move toward lighter, negative toward darker; the function automatically picks direction.
    • maxSteps: Maximum number of iterations (safety cap).
  • Returns: A new color meeting or exceeding the required contrast ratio.
mtd ensureContrast(target: Color, requiredContrast: f32 = 4.5, step: f32 = 0.02, maxSteps: s32 = 64)

func Color.relativeLuminance #src

Calculates the color's relative luminance in linear light.

Uses the linearized RGB values from Pixel.Color.toLinear and BT.709 coefficients (WCAG 2.x). Returns a scalar in [0, 1] representing perceived brightness. Formula: Y = 0.2126 R_lin + 0.7152 G_lin + 0.0722 * B_lin where R_lin, G_lin, B_lin are the linearized channels.

func Drawing.paint #src

Paints the drawing with its origin at (x, y) of the current path space, its content multiplied by scale.

Fills honor the winding of their contours (a counter-clockwise contour is a hole), strokes honor width, caps, and joins scaled by scale.

mtd const paint(painter: *Painter, x, y: f32, scale = 1.0'f32)
func Drawing.parse #src

Parses an SVG document authored in the supported subset.

The result owns its shapes and decoded images. Text supports one-level tspan runs with x, y, dx, dy, size, family class, anchor, weight, style, letter and word spacing, solid fill, and opacity, and runs along the direction its element is turned by. Images stretch into their declared rectangle. Patterns repeat vector shape tiles in user or object-bounding-box units. Filters support either a Gaussian blur followed by offsets, or a standalone feDropShadow.

A clip-path is instantiated in the space of the element that names it, a use fits a referenced symbol's view box into the size it asks for, and markers are placed on authored vertices with the tangent orientation orient="auto" states. A reference to an identifier the document does not define leaves its element alone.

options confines external image references and selects the typefaces for text; see Pixel.Svg.ParseOptions. Unknown elements and attributes are ignored.

func parse(text: string, options: ParseOptions = {})->Drawing fail
func Drawing.rasterize #src

Rasterizes the drawing into an owned image of exactly width by height pixels.

The drawing is scaled uniformly from its view box to width, antialiased, on a transparent ground. Rasterization is done in software: no window, no GPU.

supersample renders that many samples per axis and box-filters them down, replacing the renderer's screen-space edge feather with near-exact coverage. The default doubles sampling, a good balance for icon and atlas work.

An application that already owns a renderer should pass it to the overload below instead: filling the supersampled buffer is the whole cost here, and a GPU backend does it in a fraction of the time.

mtd const rasterize(width, height: s32, supersample: u8 = 2)->Image

Rasterizes the drawing through renderer into an owned image of exactly width by height pixels.

The result is identical whichever backend produces it, up to the raster-edge tolerance the two backends already carry elsewhere. Supersampled work is split into aligned tiles, so the renderer never retains a target larger than 1024 by 1024 samples; only the finished image crosses back to the caller.

The renderer must be ready to draw — its context selected and Pixel.IRenderer.init called — because this records a complete painter submission and executes it.

mtd const rasterize(renderer: IRenderer, width, height: s32, supersample: u8 = 2)->Image

func FillPreparer.flatten #src

Flattens a path for a draw at scale, without tessellating anything.

A stroked path is turned into geometry by the frame that draws it, so there is no tessellation to build for one; flattening it here still keeps the frame from doing it.

mtd flatten(pathList: *LinePathList, scale: f32, quality = PaintQuality.Normal)
func FillPreparer.prepare #src

Prepares what Pixel.Painter.fillPath under rule would build for pathList.

scale is the number of device pixels one path unit covers, the way Pixel.Painter.setFlattenScale reads it, and is quantized the same way: ask for the scale the shape will be drawn at, and the frame that draws it finds everything cached. Asking for less leaves the frame to flatten the geometry again; asking for more only costs the extra segments.

func Font.opticalLineTop #src

Y of the top of a line box of this font whose capitals are centered on centerY.

This is how a single line is centered in something a reader sees the edges of — a field, a cell, a button. Centering the line box instead hands the placement to the internal leading of the face: two fields of one form, one set in the interface face and one in the fixed-width one, then put their words on centers a couple of pixels apart, and neither on the center of the frame around it. What the eye compares is the ink, so it is the ink that is centered.

mtd const opticalLineTop(centerY: f32)->f32
func Font.opticalOffset #src

Distance from the middle of a line box to the middle of the text a reader sees in it.

A line box reaches from the ascender to the descender, but a word is read on its capitals, and the two middles are not the same point: the ascender keeps room above the capitals for accents the word may not carry, and the descender keeps room below the baseline for tails it may not carry either. The sign therefore belongs to the face, not to the rule — a text face with generous accent room reads low in its line box, a compact one reads high. Add it to the center of a rectangle a single line box is centered in to place anything that has to look level with that line, such as a leading icon or a check mark.

mtd const opticalOffset()->f32

func Font.resolveDrawFont #src

Resolves the concrete font for an on-screen pixel size.

effectivePx is the glyph size in physical device pixels, including zoom and display scale. An MSDF font returns itself: it is size independent. A bitmap font re-rasterizes at the effective size when it differs from its own, so the atlas always matches the device pixels it lands on. An automatic font uses the size-independent MSDF view at or above the automatic quality threshold, and a crisp bitmap rasterized at the exact device pixel size below it.

func Image.keyOutGround #src

Turns the flat ground of a two-color mark into transparency, keeping the glyph.

A product mark ships flattened — one glyph over one ground — because that is what a taskbar, a file list, and an installer need. Drawn over a surface that already has a ground of its own, that tile reads as a box around the glyph rather than as the mark.

Every pixel is read as a blend of the two declared colors: how far it has travelled from ground towards foreground becomes its alpha, and its color becomes foreground. The antialiased rim of the glyph therefore survives as a soft edge instead of collapsing into a staircase. A pixel that is neither — a mark that carries a third color — keeps whatever share of the two it projects onto, which is the most an operation with two colors to go on can honestly say.

A format without an alpha channel has nowhere to put the result and is left as is.

mtd keyOutGround(ground, foreground: Color)

func Image.setTransparentColor #src

Replaces the color of every fully transparent pixel with color, leaving alpha alone.

A pixel nothing covers still carries a color, and every operation that averages neighbors pulls that color into the visible edge beside it: a linear sampler minifying the image, a box downsample, a tint. Black behind a shape is exactly what gives a scaled-down sprite its dark halo, so an atlas or an icon usually wants white there, or the color of the art around it. Only pixels at alpha zero change, so what the image actually shows is untouched.

A format without an alpha channel has no fully transparent pixel and is left as is.

mtd setTransparentColor(color: Color)
func Image.smartCrop #src

Reframes and crops the image to the size of rect.

The position in rect is ignored: Pixel searches the source for the highest-scoring placement with the requested width and height. The final crop always uses the original pixels, even when search downscaling is enabled.

mtd smartCrop(rect: Math.Rectangle, opts: SmartCropSearchOpts = {})
func Image.toHicon #src

Creates a Windows icon from this image while preserving its logical color channels and alpha.

mtd toHicon()->HICON fail
func Image.visitPixels #src

Visits pixels in parallel using chunks separated by stride pixels.

stride must be positive. Each injected invocation receives:

pixaddress of the pixel
imagethe processed image
indexthe pixel index
xthe pixel x coordinates
ythe pixel y coordinates
userDataas passed to the macro
#[Swag.Macro] mtd visitPixels(pixelUserData: #null *void = null, stride: s32 = 1, stmt: #code(var pix, image, index: u64, x: s32, y: s32, userData))

func ImageCanvas.clear #src

Lays a solid ground under the drawing recorded so far.

The ground is written with alpha enabled, so a canvas can produce either an opaque image or one that keeps its transparency, and it is remembered for the frames that follow.

mtd clear(color: Color)
func ImageCanvas.create #src

Opens an off-screen canvas with positive dimensions.

The canvas starts cleared to fully transparent.

func create(width, height: s32)->ImageCanvas fail

Opens a canvas over an existing image, to draw on top of it.

The image is uploaded once and laid down under every frame, so the recorded drawing composites over it exactly as it would over a window's previous content. The source image itself is never modified; each read returns a new one.

Example

var photo = try Image.load("photo.png") var canvas = try ImageCanvas.create(photo) canvas.painter.drawString(&font, 8, 8, "caption", Color.fromRgb(255, 255, 255)) var stamped = try canvas.toImage()
func create(image: Image)->ImageCanvas fail

func Layer.releaseImmediate #src

Returns every owned render target straight to the renderer pool and resets the layer.

Pixel.Layer.release records the release into the painter command stream, which is right in the middle of a frame but wrong for a layer retained across frames: Pixel.Painter.begin discards pending commands, so a release recorded between two frames would be lost with them. Call this form instead when releasing a retained layer, once no recorded frame still draws from its targets.

func LinePath.controlBounds #src

Returns the rectangle enclosing every point that defines this path.

A Bézier is contained by its control polygon and an arc by its centre and radii, so this answers without flattening anything: it works on a path still being built, and costs one pass over the segments. The result can be wider than the ink the path finally lays down, and is never narrower — which is what makes it safe to reject work against, and unsuitable for measuring a drawing.

if !path.controlBounds().intersects(dirtyRect) do return
mtd const controlBounds()->Math.Rectangle

func LinePath.flatten #src

Convert the path to a list of points

scale is the number of device pixels one path unit covers when the result is drawn: the flattening tolerance is expressed in path units, so a curve zoomed by a transform needs proportionally more segments to look as smooth on screen as it does at scale one. The cache keeps the finest flattening produced so far, whichever combination of quality and scale asked for it.

mtd flatten(quality = PaintQuality.Normal, scale = 1.0'f32)

Clears the path and starts a new open contour at (startX, startY).

func LinePath.transform #src

Maps every point of the path through an affine transform, in place.

Lines and Bézier segments map exactly. An arc does not survive an affine map — a rotation or a skew turns it into an elliptical arc this representation cannot express — so an arc is first rewritten as the cubic Bézier segments that trace it, and those are mapped. The flattened geometry is discarded; the path flattens again the next time it is painted.

clip.transform(placement.inverse())
mtd transform(transform: Math.Transform2)
func LinePathList.clean #src

Unions and normalizes groups of already-flattened paths.

rule decides which regions of a self-overlapping or multi-contour group count as interior. The default treats a nonzero winding count as filled, which is what the clockwise-outer, anticlockwise-hole convention of this type expresses; pass EvenOdd for geometry authored under the alternating rule, where two overlapping contours of the same direction cancel instead of merging.

mtd clean(rule = Clipper.PolyFillType.NonZero)

Releases and removes all owned paths.

mtd clear()
func LinePathList.controlBounds #src

Returns the rectangle enclosing every point that defines the owned paths.

This is the union of each path's Pixel.LinePath.controlBounds, and shares its properties: it needs no flattening, it can be wider than the ink, and it is never narrower. An empty list answers an empty rectangle.

mtd const controlBounds()->Math.Rectangle
func LinePathList.count #src

Returns the number of owned paths.

#[Swag.Inline] mtd const count() => .paths
func LinePathList.flatten #src

Flattens all paths at quality and recomputes combined bounds.

scale is the number of device pixels one path unit covers when the result is drawn; see Pixel.LinePath.flatten.

mtd flatten(quality: PaintQuality = .Normal, scale = 1.0'f32)
func LinePathList.intersect #src

Keeps the regions of this already-flattened list that also lie inside clip.

rule says which regions of this list count as interior and clipRule says the same for clip, so a ring authored under the alternating rule clips as a ring. Both lists must be flattened first, the way Pixel.LinePathList.clean requires, and the result is normalized the same way: outer contours clockwise, each followed by its own holes. A clip that shares no region with the list leaves it empty.

shape.flatten(.High) frame.flatten(.High) shape.intersect(&frame)
mtd intersect(clip: *LinePathList, rule = Clipper.PolyFillType.NonZero, clipRule = Clipper.PolyFillType.NonZero)

func Painter.capStyleExtent #src

Returns the extent of a cap in the frame of the line it terminates.

lineSize is the stroke width the cap is measured against, and capScaleX/capScaleY are the scales the pen applies to an anchor. w is how far the cap stands across the line and l how far it reaches past the point it is placed on; an arrow head answers zero for l, because its tip is that point and its body lies back along the line.

These are the two axes of the line, not of the drawing. A layer or a cell reserving room around a cap wants Pixel.Painter.capStyleRadius instead, unless it knows which way the line runs.

func capStyleExtent(capStyle: LineCapStyle, lineSize, capScaleX: f32, capScaleY: f32 = 2)->{ w: f32, l: f32 }
func Painter.capStyleRadius #src

Returns how far a cap reaches from the point it is placed on, in any direction.

A cap stands across its line as well as along it, so its far corner sits at the diagonal of the two and lands anywhere on the drawing depending on which way the line runs. This is the radius that holds it whatever that direction is, which is what an axis-aligned box around the geometry has to reserve: measured from the two axes alone, that box cuts the corner off a square end or an arrow head as soon as the line stops being axis aligned.

func capStyleRadius(capStyle: LineCapStyle, lineSize, capScaleX: f32, capScaleY: f32 = 2)->f32

func Painter.computeLayout #src

Recompute the layout for a given rectangle

deviceScale must match the scale the text is drawn with. Chunk widths are measured with the same resolved draw font and device-snapped advances the draw pass uses, so wrapped lines, alignment, and inter-chunk gaps land where the glyphs actually end; measuring with nominal advances instead lets a per-glyph drift accumulate until a space between two chunks visually vanishes.

func computeLayout(pos: Math.Rectangle, text: *RichString, format: RichStringFormat, deviceScale = 1.0'f32)
func Painter.computeTextDrawInfo #src

Resolves the bitmap or MSDF font, pixel snapping, and scale for a draw.

zoom and transformScale are multiplicative and must be positive for meaningful output. transformScale is the number of physical device pixels one drawing unit covers on screen; pass the surface's device scale (or Pixel.Painter.textTransformScale when drawing through a painter) so an automatic font resolves against the real on-screen glyph size.

func computeTextDrawInfo(font: *Font, zoom = 1.0'f32, transformScale = 1.0'f32)->TextDrawInfo

Fill a list of paths. If the path is clockwise, it will be filled. If the path is anti-clockwise, it will be considered as a hole.

mtd fillPath(pathList: *LinePathList, brush: Brush)

Fills a list of paths under an explicitly named fill rule.

The plain Pixel.Painter.fillPath reads the winding direction of each contour: a clockwise one adds ink and an anticlockwise one takes it away. That is a convenient convention for geometry authored for it, but it is not what a vector document format means. PDF and SVG state a rule over the winding count, and under it a glyph drawn as outlines fills correctly whichever direction its contours happen to run — which is exactly the case the direction convention gets wrong, filling in the counter of every letter whose outer contour runs the unexpected way.

The geometry is normalized under rule before it is filled, so the result is the region the rule defines rather than the one the directions suggest.

painter.fillPath(&glyph, brush, .NonZero)
mtd fillPath(pathList: *LinePathList, brush: Brush, rule: PathFillRule)

Fills a list of paths under an explicitly named fill rule with a solid color.

func Painter.setContentScale #src

Sets the number of physical device pixels per painter path-space unit.

Drawing keeps using logical units: the renderer scales every recorded coordinate at draw time, while antialiasing fringes, text resolution, and device-grid snapping account for the real on-screen pixel size. 1, the default, draws one path-space unit per device pixel. The value survives Pixel.Painter.begin; set it once per owner, or per pass when a frame mixes logical and physical passes.

mtd setContentScale(scale: f32)

func Painter.setFlattenScale #src

Sets how many device pixels one path-space unit covers for curve flattening.

Flattening tolerances are expressed in path units, so a consumer that zooms vector geometry through its transform — a document viewer scaling a page — declares the zoom here and curves stay as smooth on screen as they are at scale one. The value is quantized to the power of two below it, between a sixty-fourth and sixty-four, so the derived caches re-key on zoom buckets rather than on every wheel step. 1, the default, keeps the calibrated path-space tolerances untouched. Set it per pass and restore it, the way Pixel.Painter.setContentScale is managed.

Below one it declares a minified pass, where a path unit covers less than a device pixel: round joins and caps take fewer segments, and a stroke walks its contour in steps of one tolerance rather than visiting points a shared pixel could not tell apart. Curve flattening itself is never coarsened — a cached contour keeps the finest tessellation anything asked of it, so the result cannot depend on the order two consumers reached the same geometry.

mtd setFlattenScale(scale: f32)

func Painter.startClippingRegion #src

Starts drawing a clipping region, which begins empty.

Until Pixel.Painter.endClippingRegion, what is drawn shades nothing: its coverage — the antialiased edge, the alpha of a texture, the transparency of a colour — joins the region under mode instead. Everything painted after that, up to Pixel.Painter.resetClippingRegion, is cut by the region's coverage per device pixel, so a shape cut along a curve keeps a smooth edge. A render target bound inside a region is not cut while it is being painted; the region applies to the layer when it is drawn.

painter.startClippingRegion() painter.fillRoundRect(frame, 12, 12, Argb.White) painter.endClippingRegion() painter.drawTexture(frame, photo) painter.resetClippingRegion()

func Svg.trace #src

Traces a flat-color raster image into a vector document.

Pixels are grouped by color; each group's coverage is contour-traced with sub-pixel precision on the antialiased alpha boundary, simplified, and written as one filled shape per color, in back-to-front coverage order. The result is faithful for the flat-color art this is meant for — icon glyphs, UI masks — and approximate for photographs, which have no flat regions to trace.

Example

let image = try Image.load("icon.png") let doc = Svg.trace(&image) try doc.save("icon.svg")
func trace(image: const *Image, options: TraceOptions = {})->Document

func Testing.assertGolden #src

Compares the display list recorded by painter against the golden named name.

The painter is serialized with Testing.dumpPainter, so this asserts on the commands a drawing emits, not on the pixels it would produce: it needs no GPU and no window, and its result is identical on every machine.

Goldens live in a goldens folder next to the calling source file, one .txt file per name. name may contain / to group goldens in sub-folders.

There is no recording mode and no flag to pass. A name with no golden yet writes one and passes, so a new test starts by producing its reference; the file then shows up as untracked, which is where it gets reviewed and committed. A name whose golden no longer matches writes the produced text next to it as <name>.actual.txt, prints the first differing line, and fails. Accepting the new output is therefore a copy, which swc tools/goldens.swgs does in bulk.

Both writes land in the module source tree, which a sandboxed run reaches only through the corpus 'swc test' grants it. See Core.Env.grantCorpus.

func assertGolden(painter: const *Painter, name: string, level = DumpLevel.Full, loc = #callerlocation)
func Testing.assertGoldenText #src

Compares arbitrary text against the golden named name.

Behaves exactly like Testing.assertGolden but takes the snapshot text directly, for callers that build their own normalized representation. Both sides are compared with end of lines normalized to \n, so a CRLF checkout never changes the outcome.

func assertGoldenText(text: string, name: string, loc = #callerlocation)
func Testing.assertImageGolden #src

Compares owned pixels against the PNG golden named name.

Goldens live beside the calling test under goldens/<name>.png. A missing golden is created and passes, like Testing.assertGolden. A mismatch writes <name>.actual.png, reports its first differing pixel, and fails. Testing.ImageGoldenOptions can tolerate bounded codec or raster differences; both limits default to exact comparison.

func assertImageGolden(image: const *Image, name: string, options: ImageGoldenOptions = {}, loc = #callerlocation)
func Testing.assertImagesNear #src

Compares two owned pixel buffers with the same bounded tolerance as image goldens.

expected and actual must be valid images. Dimensions must match exactly. A channel delta at or below Pixel.Testing.ImageGoldenOptions.maxChannelDelta is accepted; at most Pixel.Testing.ImageGoldenOptions.maxDifferentPixels pixels may exceed it. A failed comparison writes <name>.expected.png and <name>.actual.png beside the calling test.

func assertImagesNear(expected, actual: const *Image, name: string, options: ImageGoldenOptions = {}, loc = #callerlocation)
func Testing.dumpPainter #src

Serializes the display list recorded by painter into a stable, human readable snapshot.

The result is meant to be stored as a golden file and compared verbatim, so every value that is not reproducible across runs or machines is normalized away:

  • Texture handles, font and render target addresses, and shader uniform locations are replaced by tex#N, font#N, rt#N, shader#N and p#N indices assigned in first-use order.
  • Font labels keep only the file name of the underlying typeface, never its directory.
  • Floating point values are rounded to three decimals and printed without an exponent.

The snapshot opens with one # legend line per remapped object, then a blank line, then one line per command. Lines are separated by a single \n and the result ends with a \n.

painter must have completed a begin() / end() pass; the painter is only read, never modified. A lower level keeps snapshots of composite drawings (widgets, whole windows) readable while still catching command level regressions.

func dumpPainter(painter: const *Painter, level = DumpLevel.Full)->String

func TypeFace.exists #src

Reports whether Pixel.TypeFace.load has a font to load for fullname.

A caller choosing among several families needs a miss to be an answer rather than a failure: a machine that does not carry the requested face still has to draw its text, and asking here is how it moves on to the next candidate. The lookup follows the same order load does, so an answer of true is one load honors.

func exists(fullname: string)->bool

func Yuv420View.convertRowsToRgb #src

Converts rows firstY until endY into an RGB8 target of the same geometry.

Bands write disjoint destination rows, so they run concurrently on one target.

mtd const convertRowsToRgb(target: *Image, firstY, endY: s32)
func Yuv420View.convertToRgb #src

Converts the picture into target, which is created or reused as RGB8.

Bands of rows are independent, so the work fans through the scheduler when one is running. A caller drawing through a renderer should not need this at all: converting a large picture costs more processor time than decoding it, and a renderer converts where it draws.

mtd const convertToRgb(target: *Image)
